youtube_title: If a Monkey Takes the Photo, Who Owns the Copyright?
caption: The U.S. Copyright Office won't register works produced by animals — and its own rulebook lists 'a photo taken by a monkey' as an example. Owning the camera isn't the same as being the author.
script: A monkey took a selfie, and the U.S. Copyright Office won't register it for anyone. Not the photographer. Not the monkey. [disclaimer] Meet a photographer. He sets up a camera in the jungle, and walks away for a minute. A monkey grabs the camera. And snaps a perfect selfie. The photographer says, great, it's my camera, so it's my photo. But in America, the Copyright Office has a rulebook. It won't register work made by nature, animals, or plants. And it gives examples. A photo taken by a monkey. A painting made by an elephant. Driftwood shaped by the ocean. Wait. So the monkey owns it? You see, copyright protects creative work made by humans. Only humans. Owning the camera doesn't make you the author, just like owning a pen doesn't make you the writer of every note someone scribbles with it. This doesn't mean every animal photo is free. If a person picks the shot, the angle and the moment, that's a human author. And other countries can see it differently. So the photographer owns the camera. He owns the memory card. He owns the trip. And the best photo he ever got is the one photo the Copyright Office won't register for anybody. Not him. Not the monkey. script_old: If a monkey takes the photo, who gets the copyright? Under U.S. law, the answer is awkward. The U.S. Copyright Office has a rulebook for what it will register, called the Compendium. And it says plainly: the Office will not register works produced by nature, animals, or plants. Then it gives examples. A photo taken by a monkey. A mural painted by an elephant. Driftwood shaped and smoothed by the ocean. Even a song application that names the Holy Spirit as its author. The principle is human authorship. Copyright protects creative work by people. So imagine you set up a camera, and a monkey grabs it and snaps a picture. You may own the camera. You may own the memory card. But owning the equipment doesn't make you the author of a photo the monkey took. Here's the limit. This doesn't mean every picture with an animal in it is unprotected. A photographer who chooses the shot, the framing and the moment is a human author. When a person and an animal both play a part, the human contribution has to be looked at on its own.
